segments.text: Imagine a stock that has climbed for months, from thirty two dollars all the way to sixty.
It dips, then pushes to a new high of seventy.
But the next push only reaches sixty one. It could not even make a new high.
Then it falls through a level it had bounced off twice before.
Traders have a name for this shape. It looks like a person: two shoulders and a head.
The head and shoulders pattern.
Welcome to Math Lab TV. Where math is something you can see.
Today you will learn how to spot the three peaks.
You will see why the neckline is the line that matters.
And you will measure a price target with simple subtraction.
Let's slow down and read the chart one peak at a time.
The first peak, at sixty, is the left shoulder. Buyers are still in control.
The second peak, at seventy, is the head. It is the highest point of the whole move.
The third peak, at sixty one, is the right shoulder. It is lower than the head.
That lower high is the first warning. Buyers tried again, and they ran out of strength.
The shoulders do not need to match exactly. Real charts are never that neat.
Now look at the two dips between the peaks. Both stopped at fifty two.
Join them with a line, and you have the neckline.
Here is the key idea. Until price closes below the neckline, there is no pattern yet.
It is only a shape that might become one.
When the price closes below fifty two, the pattern is confirmed.
Volume often tells the same story. Trading is lighter on the right shoulder, then jumps on the break.
And sometimes the price comes back up to touch the neckline from below, before it falls away.
So how far might it fall? There is a simple rule of thumb.
Measure the height of the head above the neckline.
Seventy minus fifty two is eighteen dollars.
Now copy that same eighteen down from the neckline.
Fifty two minus eighteen is thirty four. That is the price target.
Traders also decide where they would be wrong. A common choice is just above the right shoulder, at sixty one.
Selling at the break, at fifty two, risks nine dollars to aim for eighteen.
That is two dollars of possible reward for every dollar of risk.
Three mistakes trip up beginners.
Mistake one: acting before the neckline breaks. Many right shoulders simply turn back up.
Mistake two: finding the shape anywhere. It is a reversal pattern, so it needs an uptrend before it to reverse.
Mistake three: treating the target as a promise. It is a rule of thumb. Price can stop short, or overshoot.
And a bonus: flip the chart upside down, and you get the inverse head and shoulders, a possible bottom after a fall.
Here is the whole recipe.
One. Start with an uptrend.
Two. Find three peaks, with the head the highest.
Three. Draw the neckline through the two dips.
Four. Wait for a close below it.
Five. Measure the head, copy it down, and set where you would be wrong.
A pattern is not a prediction. It is a way to plan your risk.
Look around your world, and notice how often a rally runs out of steam before it turns.
If this lesson made things clear for you, please subscribe to Math Lab TV, so we can keep building together.
But here's a puzzle for next time.
What if the price makes only two peaks, at the same height? That is the double top.
I will see you in the next video.
